title: 🛒 Retail vibe check
body_text: It is a modern age of miracles with the dawn of AI, and if you’re going to succeed at a time like this you’ve got to be willing to turn your business model around on a dime and deliver what the people want. Take a buzzy startup called Inception AI that used LLMs to generate 15,000 AI-generated podcasts hosted by more than 50 AI personalities to produce some 3,000 episodes a week for $1 an episode or less. The startup has cracked a brilliant, innovative, and daring new business model: just hiring human hosts . Turns out audiences liked them way more, and nobody was particularly interested in what quickly became 350,000 episodes of digital chum. Who could have thought? Stocks fell on Tuesday. After the bell, Nvidia beat on both top and bottom lines . Investors are getting a vibe check from American consumers this week, with the first big slew of data arriving after the US midterm elections, where concerns over the cost of living took center stage. Here’s a summary of some of the data Wall Street has to mull this week: US retail sales slowed in October as purchases of big ticket items like cars and furniture slipped, according to the most recent reading from the Commerce Department released Tuesday. Home improvement giant Home Depot reported sales and profit numbers that beat expectations but narrowed its profit guidance, setting the stage for its competitor Lowe’s to report on Wednesday. Both companies also face pressure from high mortgage rates. In an environment where it is harder to purchase a home, there is less reason for trips to their stores. Target will also report on Wednesday, as will TJX , the company behind the discount retailer TJ Maxx. Finally, on Thursday we get the big one: Walmart . What these companies report and what they say on their earnings calls will give investors a sense of how they are positioned going into the holiday season. And to put a bow on it, the University of Michigan’s latest Consumer Sentiment Index reading lands on Friday. The index has been hovering around historic lows this year. This data comes as a relatively resilient labor market and a stock market that, until recently, had been climbing helped keep consumers spending, particularly wealthier Americans who own stocks and other assets. Consumers are keeping the US economy chugging along, but not with a smile on their faces. Americans have been increasingly unhappy watching the price of gas and other goods go up and up while Silicon Valley types get richer and richer. And that’s increasingly not Walmart’s problem. For the past several years there’s been a growing disconnect between how much consumers are spending and their attitudes about the economy. They are still purchasing discretionary items like “Grand Theft Auto VI” while feeling pessimistic about their finances. That’s largely because employment has stayed steady. Smaller luxuries like a new videogame or a modest home renovation project are still in the budget, but buying a home, or even a car or new couch, is not. After this week investors will have a clearer picture on whether consumers are pulling back or simply getting pickier. title: 🌊 Oceans are now battlefields
body_text: There’s a new 007, and it’s none other than Robert Pattinson . The star will slip into the tux and pick up the Walther PPK after being tapped by Amazon ’s MGM and director Denis Villeneuve for the part of James Bond. Pattinson, 40, has proven wide adaptability across his career, and it’s easy to see why he’s a great fit for the part. He showed he’s capable of putting up with chaotic productions with ravenous fandoms during Twilight, he’s played an international man of mystery in Tenet and a swashbuckling explorer in The Lost City of Z, and perhaps most central to the mission of Bond, a pervasive theme of his career is a love of parts — from Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire to Queen of the Desert to Mickey 17 — where he shows a keen interest in risking life and limb to protect the interests of the British aristocracy. This morning the Walt Disney Company will report earnings. Many will focus on the Disney+ subscriber numbers, plenty of attention will be paid to how Disney will cut headcount and integrate AI tools into film development, and the bill for all those college football games and sports rights will be scrutinized to death. But what if, underneath all the movies and the streaming and the Magic™, an even more interesting bet on the future of the company is taking place at the House of Mouse? Here’s a trivia question for you: over the past six months, what company in the S&P 500 has traded with the strongest correlation to The Walt Disney Company? Perhaps a streamer, given how much emphasis the company places on Disney+ and its centrality to the “One Disney” strategy ? You’re close — Netflix trades like Disney a lot, to be sure — but not quite the No. 1 correlated stock. Perhaps some consumer discretionary staple, given how much of Disney’s Vault is filled by the proceeds from toy, doll, and apparel sales? Close, but no; though Nike , Visa and Mastercard are all up there. Maybe a peer, you think, another diversified studio: Comcast . Good guess, but that’s only the 10th most correlated, in fact. No, the single most strongly correlated stock with Disney over the past six months has been Booking Holdings , the company behind all those travel fare aggregators. And the reason for that is that Disney is a vacation sales company that, in order to drum up business, produces a couple of movies a year to chum the waters and get people into theme parks and on to cruise ships. It’s that last point, though, that is worth drawing attention to. Disney has launched two new ships, bringing its total fleet to eight vessels, and has a further five cruise ships on order to join the armada by 2031. That’s all to push double-digit growth in the Resorts and Vacations segment, which is the real profit flywheel for Disney. Last year, Experiences was responsible for 37% of revenue but fully 60% of profit , and the cruise liners are at the center of the strategy. That’s the number that lots of investors will be paying attention to on the Disney print today. What makes the investment in cruises so interesting for Disney is that it is an especially clever play given the constraints around the theme park business. These new ships are better understood less as cruise ships and more as floating theme parks that you can send anywhere in the world and which operate with a degree of sovereignty that is simply hard to get on a terrestrial park. Disney’s latest effort to build a theme park, the Shanghai park, was the result of decades of work with the Chinese government and a five-year construction process. All of which ended with a Disney park that is 57% owned by the Chinese state. If you’re Disney, are you thrilled with these constraints? Do you enjoy pretending that you never made Kundun so that you can get 43 fen on the yuan? Heck, even the American parks have their irritations. Disney once had the ability to install a nuclear reactor in Disney World if they saw fit; a fight with Gov. Ron DeSantis reminded the company that even Florida would squeeze them like an orange if given the chance. If you’re the Mouse, you’ve got six destinations — California, Florida, France, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Japan. Let’s say you want a seventh park. Where would you even put it, so that you would (a) not cannibalize your existing business and (b) have an affluent market that is geographically far from your existing footprint and (c) serves a market large enough to demand a new park? I’m sure the boys in Burbank looked long and hard at a map and came up short. There are probably not that many more markets that could sustain a seventh year-round Disney park. But what if the theme park could serve a region for half that time, or a quarter of that time, and then go to another region? You can’t do that if your park is attached to Florida. You can do that if you compress your park and put it on a boat. Local government starts getting ornery? Screw em, cancel the sailings from their ports. Incomes rising sharply in a country? Add them to the list, start with two sailings a year and then dial it up as the median income goes up. Fuel costs spiking? Just sail the park to them , after all every dollar spent on the airline ticket is a dollar the guest can’t spend at Disney. The cruise lines allow them to essentially do surge pricing, but for an amusement park, following the demand while maintaining the kind of autonomy that can truly only be found in international waters. title: 🧥 Nvidia loses its leather jacket
body_text: Happy Monday to everyone except those whose employers use Microsoft Outlook for email. Those poor souls, who already spend half their workday searching for emails that are definitely in their inboxes, got an unexpected break on Thursday and Friday thanks to a widespread Microsoft outage . They probably needed it. After all, Teams tells their bosses they're slacking off if they leave their mouse untouched for more than five minutes. Headlines last week were dominated by one thing. For those living under a rock, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following a series of bombshell reports that painted a picture of a leather jacket-clad man who founded a chip company for video games, became one of the most powerful people in the world, and apparently succumbed to the temptations that came with it. First came reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman who US intelligence officials reportedly considered a spy for the Chinese government. The woman’s company, Megaspeed, was reportedly able to obtain Nvidia chips in China despite export controls designed to prevent China from beating the US on artificial intelligence. (Oh, and during this time, he was also reportedly having affairs with at least two Nvidia employees.) Meanwhile, in Washington, they’re all trying to find the guy who was supposed to prevent this from happening but didn’t. Lawmakers called on Haung and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify. This brings into question how long Lutnick, who is supposed to be in charge of enforcing those export controls, will stay with the administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he supported blacklisting Megaspeed but Lutnick didn’t act . Secretary of State Marco Rubio (a Republican presidential hopeful), also reportedly sounded the alarms about the relationship to no avail . Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will be interim CEO. But the transition could be awkward, given that Huang didn't always seem to hold her in particularly high regard. As recently as this summer, Huang belittled her at a meeting and called her a “deer in the headlights,” according to The Wall Street Journal . When asked earlier this fall by Wired who the most powerful women in tech were, Huang did not name her. We still don’t know who will replace Huang on a permanent basis. President Trump suggested former Apple CEO, Tim Cook. Prediction markets are favoring Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing. The stock has taken a massive hit from the scandal. Nvidia is still scheduled to report earnings results on Tuesday, in which it may report better-than-expected numbers, as it often does, which could potentially offer some relief. Kress will take questions from analysts, some of whom downgraded the stock this week . The market is still figuring out how to price in this juicy gossip. On one hand, the scandal shows people want Nvidia's chips so badly that they're willing to (allegedly) commit espionage to get them. And demand for those chips isn't going to disappear just because Huang is gone. On the other hand, the allegations have invited a major legal and regulatory headache for Nvidia at a time investors have been jittery about the AI trade and the public opinion on AI infrastructure has soured. Then there's the Jensen factor. Maybe Huang, the only CEO the company has ever had, has the secret sauce that a successor won't be able to replicate. As my colleague Luke Kawa points out in the EntryPoint newsletter, Huang's interpersonal skills helped bolster demand (perhaps to a fault). The question now is whether Nvidia's next CEO can keep the orders flowing without the industry's most recognizable salesman. As the Nvidia scandal unfolded Thursday, the chip company completely dominated trading activity on Robinhood. 6,184 single stocks were traded on Robinhood Markets on Thursday, and net purchases of Nvidia were more than double the rest of those 6,183 stocks, combined!
